national.title: Zelensky says Crimean Bridge strikes 'fair response' as he meets UK's Streeting
national.summary: Ukraine's president says Kyiv acted after 109 separate Russian aerial attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
national.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

He also rejected the claim the Russian president made in China that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsular it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

national.title: Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa
national.summary: A federal court indefinitely suspended the U.S. Army's plans to detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Iowa after communities raised concerns.
national.body: A federal court on Friday suspended the U.S. Army's plans to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa after community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume across parts of Iowa and Illinois.An emergency motion was granted by the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to pause the demolition of lead azide after environmental groups filed a lawsuit.Two controlled explosions were originally scheduled for Friday at noon in Middletown, Iowa — a rural community of 360 people located about four hours from Chicago. The Army then delayed it until Monday before the court stepped in.The military had released a statement saying it was working closely with the Department of Health and Human Services and the Environmental Protection Agency to ensure the controlled explosion would be conducted in the safest manner possible. "Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement said. But why exactly does the Army need to detonate the chemicals and what are the risks to the public?Why does the Army need to detonate lead azide in Iowa?In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, told CBS News Chicago that the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather.Military officials said it's not safe to relocate the explosive materials. national.title: Recipe: Citrus-and-Butter Turkey
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: The secret to super-juicy meat and deliciously-crispy skin? (Hint: It involves a cheesecloth.)
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Justin Chapple.This citrus turkey recipe is a unique way to celebrate the start of citrus season — and a delicious, sunny addition to your holiday table. F&W's Justin Chapple also shares an easy cheesecloth trick for maximally crispy skin and succulent meat: his go-to technique for how to make the juiciest Thanksgiving turkey. Frequently Asked QuestionsWhy put lemon, orange, and grapefruit in the turkey cavity? Putting citrus inside the cavity — as well as using it to flavor the butter that's spread under the skin — will impart fragrant flavor into the entire bird. Plus, the high-water fruit will create steam as it cooks, moistening the meat from within. The pan juices will be infused with citrus, too; pour some onto your plate for an extra source of tart, aromatic goodness.What does putting butter under the skin do? Rubbing butter directly onto the meat of the bird — rather than over the skin — is a classic way to impart as much moist juiciness as possible into every part of turkey. In this case, the butter is also infused with herbs and citrus zest, so those flavors will also melt into the meat as it cooks.Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen Draping a butter-soaked cheesecloth over the breast and legs of your turkey will protect the skin from over-browning, while also maintaining moisture and keeping the flavorful citrus and thyme as close to the meat as possible. Before laying it over the bird, dampen the cheesecloth with water and then wring out any excess; this will not only prevent the cheesecloth from soaking up too much butter, but will also help prevent cloth threads from transferring onto the meat. The turkey is roasted on its own for about 30 minutes, at which point you'll pour 3 cups of chicken stock (or low-sodium broth) into the pan and continue to roast for about another hour and 45 minutes. The addition of the broth will keep the air in the oven moist — meaning a juicier turkey. Plus, you'll collect the remaining pan juices after roasting to serve over the carved meat.Citrus-and-Butter TurkeyFrom Food & Wine MagazineActive Time: 40 mins.Total Time: 2 hours 30 mins.Servings: 10-12Ingredients:1 (12 to 14-pound) turkey, rinsed and patted dryKosher saltBlack pepper1 1/2 sticks unsalted butter1 1/2 tablespoons finely grated grapefruit zest, plus 1/4 cup fresh grapefruit juice1 1/2 tablespoo

national.title: Recipe: Carla Hall's Spiced Cider-Glazed Ham
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: This holiday-worthy ham from Carla Hall glistens with a bourbon and brown sugar glaze as it fills the kitchen with a comforting aroma.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Carla Hall.The anchor of the much-anticipated holiday meal at my family's table, a lacquered and fragrant ham, was served on a large white oval china platter decorated with tiny roses. Despite being surrounded by all the fixings, the ham drew the spotlight. Whether served on the Thanksgiving table or a casual weeknight, this Spiced Cider-Glazed Ham is reminiscent of Sunday suppers at my Granny's house. Starting with a high-quality bone-in ham, such as Berkshire, is the key — the bone enhances the flavor of the meat, helps retain moisture, keeps the meat tender, and is essential to a delicious soup or pot of beans in the future. To further maximize flavor and ease of carving, opt for a spiral-cut ham. The glaze melts into the layers and gets trapped in the crevices for juicy sweetness in every bite. In the autumn months, when apples are at their peak, fresh apple cider brings rich, natural sugars and a hint of tartness that enhances the smokiness of the ham. In this recipe, the apple cider is reduced with other ingredients like bourbon (my grandmother's favorite); brown sugar, which contains molasses with a hint of bitterness and deep color; Dijon mustard that adds sharpness to the tang of the apple cider; and hearty warming spices for flavor complexity, creating a thick, syrupy glaze. The natural sugars in the cider caramelize under heat, lending a beautiful, sleek finish to the ham that is not only delicious but also visually appealing with its glossy sheen. — Carla Hall Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat is a Berkshire ham? Compared to most mainstream grocery store hams, Berkshire hams, which come from heritage-breed pigs, are well marbled and have a more meaty, concentrated flavor. How do I keep the ham from drying out? By initially covering the ham as it bakes, the meat gently soaks up the aromatic glaze, retaining its juiciness. Uncovering the ham towards the end allows the exterior to caramelize and turn golden brown, giving it a stunning crust that's not only centerpiece-worthy but also mouthwatering.Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen Spiral-cut bone-in Berkshire hams are available at specialty grocery stores or online at heritageberkshire.com.Carla Hall's Spiced Cider-Glazed HamFrom Food & Wine MagazineActive Time: 1 hour 15 mins.Total Time: 3 hoursServings: 10 Ingredients:1 (7- to 8-pound) spira

national.title: Recipe: French Onion Mac and Cheese
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Move aside, breadcrumbs! Homemade Frenched onions take mac and cheese to the next level.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Paige Grandjean.Why haven't we been putting caramelized onions in our mac and cheese all along? This is a delicious mac and cheese recipe on its own, but adding the Frenched onions is a fun way to create a sweet-savory balance — the sweet onions work so well with the sharpness of the cheese sauce. Even more enjoyable is the sourdough topping. The little "croutons" are crispy-crunchy on top and softer underneath, adding a nice texture to the creamy mac. To make the Frenched onions, sauté the onions in oil until brown and caramelized. Add in a pat of butter, a splash of sherry, and beef bouillon paste. Sprinkle them over the pasta along with buttery bread cubes for a golden-brown topping.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhat is the best cheese for mac and cheese? Use something sharp and flavorful such as cheddar, Gruyère, or Swiss cheese. These will melt easily, creating an ooey-gooey cheese sauce that will perfectly coat the noodles.What seasonings go well in mac and cheese? Salt and freshly ground black pepper are essentials, but add a combination of freshly ground nutmeg, cayenne pepper, and mustard powder (or Dijon mustard) to enhance the flavor of the cheese sauce. Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen Any short pasta, such as penne, gemelli, or campanelle, will work in place of cavatappi. national.title: Recipe: Orechiette with Brussels Sprouts & Pancetta
national.summary: From Hitchcock Farms: A pasta dish recipe featuring one of their favorite vegetables.
national.body: Hitchcock Farms, in Salinas, Calif., has been growing Brussels sprouts for generations (including purple Brussels sprouts, available seasonally). They offer "Sunday Morning" viewers this pasta dish featuring one of their favorite vegetables. Orechiette with Brussels Sprouts & PancettaFrom Hitchcock FarmsServings: 4Total Time: 30 mins. Ingredients:2 Tbsp. olive oil, divided 2 lb. Brussels sprouts, trimmed, outer leaves peeled for use, cores saved for later 1/2 lb. dried orecchiette pasta 2 oz. pancetta (Italian bacon), finely chopped 1 shallot, finely chopped 1/2 cup heavy cream 1/3 cup grated pecorino romano cheese, plus more for garnish Kosher salt Fresh ground pepperDirections:Generously salt a large pot of water and set to boil over high heat. Heat a medium sautée pan over medium-high heat for 2 minutes. Swirl in 1 Tablespoon olive oil and fry Brussels sprouts leaves until tender and starting to brown in spots, about 5 minutes. Remove brussels sprouts and set aside. Return pan to medium heat and add remaining oil, pancetta and shallots. Cook for about 4 minutes until starting to crisp and caramelize. Add cream and reduce on low. Meanwhile, cook pasta to al dente, about 12 minutes, and strain, reserving at least 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Once cream mixture has thickened and darkened a little in color, add pecorino to pan and stir to combine. Add 1/2 cup pasta cooking liquid and pasta to pan, stirring to coat, adding more pasta water as necessary to create a silky sauce. Add Brussels sprout leaves to pan and cook about 2 minutes. Taste for seasoning and add kosher salt and fresh cracked pepper as desired. Serve with additional pecorino cheese and fresh cracked pepper to garnish. Recipe by Hitchcock Farms. national.title: Recipe: Macaroni & Cheese by Good Culture
national.summary: A creamy, flavorful and cheesy mac & cheese with a boost of protein from using cottage cheese.
national.body: Good Culture Cottage Cheese shares with "Sunday Morning" viewers their take on a traditional favorite: A mac & cheese that is creamy, flavorful and cheesy, but lighter and with a boost of protein by using cottage cheese. Macaroni & CheeseFrom Good Culture Cottage CheeseServings: 8-12Ingredients:Macaroni & Cheese 8 ounces small pasta (macaroni, elbows, shells) (227 grams)1 cup Good Culture Cottage Cheese (220 grams)½ cup whole milk (120 grams)½ tsp saltFew grinds of fresh black pepper¼ tsp garlic powder¼ tsp onion powder¼ tsp paprika2 tsps cornstarch1 cup sharp cheddar cheese, shredded (113 grams)Cheesy Topping 1 cup shredded cheddar cheese (113 g)½ cup grated Parmesan cheese (45–50 g)Directions:Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Butter a baking dish.Bring a pot of salted water to a boil. Add the pasta and cook according to the package directions until just al dente. Reserve about ½ cup of pasta water, then drain the pasta and set aside.Add the cottage cheese, milk, salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, and cornstarch to a blender. Blend until completely smooth.Pour the sauce into a saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the 1 cup of shredded cheddar and stir gently until melted and the sauce is smooth and hot. Avoid letting it boil vigorously.Add the drained pasta to the sauce and stir until evenly coated. The mac and cheese should look slightly saucier than you want the finished dish to be, since the oven will thicken it. If needed, stir in a little reserved pasta water to loosen the sauce.Transfer the mac and cheese to the buttered baking dish. Evenly sprinkle the remaining 1 cup of shredded cheddar and ½ cup of Parmesan over the top.Bake uncovered for 15-20 minutes, until the cheese is melted and the edges are bubbling.Broil for an additional 1-3 minutes, watching carefully, until the topping is golden and lightly crispy.Let the mac and cheese rest for 5 minutes before serving.Once cooled, refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container.To reheat, add a couple of tablespoons of milk or water to help loosen the sauce. Microwave until heated through, stopping every soften to stir. Add a little extra liquid if needed. Recipe by Good Culture. national.title: Recipe: 'Fuskie Fried Crab and Shrimp Rice
national.summary: James Beard Award-winner Sallie Ann Robinson, born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors.
national.body: In her 2019 cookbook "Sallie Ann Robinson's Kitchen: Food and Family Lore from the Lowcountry" (published by University Press of Florida), Sallie Ann Robinson, a chef and food writer born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors. She offers "Sunday Morning" viewers her fried rice recipe.'Fuskie Fried Crab and Shrimp Riceby Sallie Ann Robinson Serves 6-8Ingredients:1 ½ cups long-grain white rice1 teaspoon salt4 tablespoons vegetable oil3 slices bacon1/3 green bell pepper, diced1/3 red bell pepper, diced½ rib celery, diced1 large onion, diced4 ounces lump crabmeat4 ounces claw crabmeat½ pound medium-size raw shrimp, peeled and deveined1 tablespoon minced garlicSalt and pepper to tasteDirections:In a large stockpot, wash and drain the rice several times, then add 2 ½ cups water and the salt. Stir to combine, cover, and cook over medium heat for 30 to 45 minutes, or until the rice is tender. In a large skillet over medium heat, fry the bacon until crisp. Remove from the skillet and set aside, leaving the bacon grease in the pan. Add 2 tablespoons oil to the pan, along with the bell peppers, celery, and onion, and cook for 3 minutes, or until the vegetables have softened. Transfer the vegetables to a bowl and set aside. Add the remaining 2 tablespoons oil to the skillet over high heat, then add the crabmeat and sauté, stirring occasionally, for 3 to 5 minutes, until the crabmeat begins to brown. Add the shrimp and the rice to the crabmeat, and stir together for 2 minutes, or until well combined and the shrimp is cooked through. Stir the sautéed vegetables and the garlic into the rice and heat through. Season with salt and pepper. Serve hot in bowls. From "Sallie Ann Robinson's Kitchen: Food and Family Lore from the Lowcountry" by Sallie Ann Robinson. Copyright 2019 by Sallie Ann Robinson. Published by University Press of Florida. national.title: Recipe: Apple Cider Risotto with Bacon and Butternut Squash
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Apple cider replaces white wine in this fall take on creamy butternut risotto.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was developed by Nicole Hopper and written by Breana Lai Killeen.This ultra-rich and creamy risotto gets a touch of sweetness, thanks to butternut squash, and subtle tartness from Granny Smith apple to balance it out. Bacon drippings coat the arborio rice, lending a slightly smoky and deeply savory flavor infused into every grain. The rice is cooked just a hair past al dente so that it's tender but still has the slightest bite and chew to it. Half the roasted butternut and apple mixture gets pureed and stirred into the risotto (the other half is reserved for topping), and a hefty amount of Parmesan and a little butter at the end add even more umami and make it nicely glossy and extra creamy. Serve the risotto with roast chicken or pork tenderloin, or a zingy arugula salad. Frequently Asked QuestionsWhy use cider instead of wine in this risotto? Apple cider gives risotto a subtle acidity, but also a bit of sweetness and fruitiness compared to a dry white wine. Try using a dry or off-dry cider instead of a sweet cider to make sure the dish doesn't become too sweet. What not to do when making risotto?A common misconception about risotto is that it takes a long time to make and that you'll be standing over the stove for an hour. In reality, the time spent cooking arborio rice should not exceed 20 minutes. If you're cooking your rice any longer than that, it will be overcooked, blown out, and mushy. And while there are other steps before adding the rice that take a little time (in this case, cooking the bacon and aromatics), it's still easily achievable in under an hour from start to finish. Can you use other types of squash?Absolutely. Any type of winter squash, such as honeynut, kabocha, or pumpkin will work well instead of butternut. Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen To nail the timing, make sure you start cooking the risotto as soon as your butternut goes into the oven. Once the vegetables are in the oven, start step 2 concurrently; everything should line right up so that you can make the puree and stir it in as soon as the rice is ready. Do not rinse your rice! For risotto, we want all that starch on the rice to make it nice and creamy, so don't wash it down the drain. national.title: Recipe: Sea Island Okra Gumbo by Sallie Ann Robinson
national.summary: The James Beard Award-winner, born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors.
national.body: In her 2003 book "Gullah Home Cooking the Daufuskie Way," Sallie Ann Robinson, a chef and food writer born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors. She offers "Sunday Morning" viewers her recipe for Okra Gumbo. Sea Island Okra Gumboby Sallie Ann Robinson Ingredients:2 pieces ham hock3 pieces fresh pig tail1-2 cans diced or stewed tomatoes4-5 cups water3 cups okra, cut up1 cup shrimp, peeled and deveinedCorn, green beans (optional)Directions:Put the pig tail and ham hock in a medium pot, half full with water. Boil 20 minutes, then drain. This will clean the meat. Rinse the meat again, twice. Return the meat to the pot, add the tomatoes (more or less, as you prefer) and 4 to 5 cups of water, and boil slowly until the meat is tender and tomatoes break down in the soup (30 to 60 minutes). If you wish, prefry the okra with a dash of oil to reduce the slime. Add the okra, prefried or not, along with shrimp, to the tomatoes and meat. If you like, add corn, green beans, or any other vegetable, canned or fresh. Cook for another 20 to 30 minutes over medium heat. Serve as a soup, over rice, or with stiff grits. From "Gullah Home Cooking the Daufuskie Way" by Sallie Ann Robinson. Copyright 2003 by Sallie Ann Robinson. Published by University of North Carolina Press. Reprinted by permission. national.title: Recipe: Sheet Pan Chicken, Brussels Sprouts & Acorn Squash
national.summary: From Hitchcock Farms: This chicken entrée recipe offers a place of pride for one of their favorite vegetables.
national.body: Hitchcock Farms, in Salinas, Calif., has been growing Brussels sprouts for generations (including purple Brussels sprouts, available seasonally). They offer "Sunday Morning" viewers this chicken entrée recipe that offers a place of pride for one of their favorite vegetables. Sheet Pan Chicken, Brussels Sprouts & Acorn SquashFrom Hitchcock FarmsServings: 4Total Time: 30 mins. Ingredients:4 bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs 1 lb. purple or green Brussels sprouts, halved 1 acorn squash, halved, seeded and cut into 1/2 in thick slices 4 shallots, quartered through the stem Olive oil Kosher salt 1/2 teaspoon chili flakes 1 Tablespoon soy sauce 1 Tablespoon honey 1 Tablespoon butter 1/4 teaspoon Chinese five spice Fresh rosemary sprigs Fresh thyme sprigsDirections:Preheat the oven to 400°. Pile the Brussels sprouts, squash and a few sprigs each of fresh thyme and rosemary together in the center of a sheet pan. Sprinkle with olive oil, 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt and chili flakes. Remove chicken from package and pat dry with paper towels. Place chicken thighs skin side up on sheet pan and space vegetables out evenly around them. Drizzle olive oil over chicken thighs and sprinkle with kosher salt. Bake for 20 minutes. Meanwhile, combine soy sauce, honey, butter and Chinese five spice in a small saucepan and heat over low heat, whisking to incorporate as butter melts. Remove sheet pan from oven and use a pastry brush to brush some of the sauce mixture over chicken. Drizzle the remainder over vegetables in pan. Return to oven and bake for another 20 minutes, until chicken skin is crispy and vegetables are caramelized. Garnish with fresh rosemary. Recipe by Hitchcock Farms. national.title: Recipe: Chai-Spiced Pumpkin Pie
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Black tea and homemade chai masala give this silky pumpkin pie an aromatic depth, while a crisp gingersnap crust and pistachio-rose garnish make it ready for the holiday table.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was developed by Maneet Chauhan and written by Breana Killeen.Pumpkin pie is often defined by warm baking spices, and Maneet Chauhan's version goes above and beyond. Her homemade chai masala combines green cardamom, fennel, cloves, cinnamon, black pepper, and star anise, adding licorice-like notes. The blend seasons both the buttery gingersnap–graham cracker crust and the pumpkin filling, so every bite carries its fragrance. This pie has the flavor and polish to stand out at a holiday gathering while still feeling unmistakably homemade. Toast and grind the chai masala shortly before baking for the brightest flavor, then cool and chill the pie completely. Served cold, each slice cuts neatly and lets the black tea, ginger, and spices shine.Tips for the best crustFor a sturdy crust with an even edge, grind the cookies and crackers to fine, uniform crumbs, then mix until every crumb is coated with butter. Use the flat bottom of a measuring cup to compact the mixture firmly across the base before pressing it up the sides. Baking the crust before filling sets its structure and heightens its toasted flavor. Let it cool completely so the crust does not begin cooking the custard unevenly. Homemade chai masala To make chai masala, combine 1/4 cup green cardamom pods, 2 tablespoons fennel seeds, 2 teaspoons whole cloves, 2 teaspoons ground ginger, 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, 1/2 teaspoon black peppercorns, and 1 star anise pod in a small skillet. Toast over medium, stirring frequently, until very fragrant, about 3 minutes. Transfer to a spice grinder to cool, then grind into a powder. Premade chai seasoning For a shortcut, use a premade chai masala in place of the homemade blend. Diaspora Co.'s Chai Spice is a caffeine-free mix of green cardamom, ginger, fennel, cinnamon, black pepper, and cloves; Spicewalla also sells a versatile Chai Masala, while Burlap & Barrel's Chai adds lemongrass and orange peel. Check the label before buying as you'll want to choose an unsweetened, tea-free ground spice blend for baking rather than a chai latte mix or a blend containing black tea. national.title: Recipe: Hastkaka ("Speed Cake")
national.summary: Sofia Draco, who operates Bun Bun Bakery out of her home in Highland Park, Calif., offers "Sunday Morning" viewers a treasured family recipe.
national.body: Sofia Draco operates Bun Bun Bakery out of her home in Highland Park, Calif., delivering her freshly-baked pastries to loyal customers. She offers "Sunday Morning" viewers a treasured cake recipe passed down to her by her grandmother, Gertrud Johansson.Draco writes:I'm sharing my grandmother's own hastkaka, which means "speed cake." You can whip up the batter in a few minutes and add whatever fruit is in season. I love it with something tart, like red currants, rhubarb, or apples tossed with cardamom, cinnamon, and sugar. It's especially good served warm with a scoop of vanilla ice cream or a quick whipped vanilla sauce. I still have the recipe in her handwriting, and I make it all the time.My Grandmother's Hastkaka ("Speed Cake")by Sofia DracoIngredients:2 eggs1 cup granulated sugar75 g butter, melted (or 5 ⅓ tablespoons)1 cup all-purpose flourSeasonal fruit, enough to scatter over the batterButter and fine breadcrumbs for the panDirections:Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Butter a cake pan, preferably a springform pan, and dust it with fine breadcrumbs.Quickly stir together the eggs, sugar, and melted butter. Add the flour and stir just until combined.Pour the batter into the prepared pan and scatter the fruit evenly over the top.Bake for 20 minutes (it can be a little sticky in the center). Serve warm with vanilla ice cream or a quick, cold whipped vanilla sauce. Quick Whipped Vanilla SauceI love serving the cake warm with this cold vanilla sauce. It takes just a few minutes to make and is best spooned over the cake right away.Ingredients: 2 egg yolks2 tablespoons granulated sugar1 teaspoon vanilla sugar, or vanilla bean paste to taste¾ cup heavy whipping creamMethod:Whisk the egg yolks, sugar, and vanilla for about 5 minutes, until pale and fluffy. national.title: Recipe: Nigella's Sticky Toffee Pudding
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: In her take on this iconic dessert, Nigella Lawson folds softened dates into a tender sponge cake that becomes irresistibly sticky after soaking up a rich brown sugar and molasses toffee sauce.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Nigella Lawson and written by Molly McArdle.Rich and sweet, from dates, molasses, and dark brown sugar, this cake from Nigella Lawson's 2018 cookbook At My Table: A Celebration of Home Cooking is a particularly indulgent dessert — and a Food & Wine Test Kitchen favorite. A generous drizzle of heavy cream (or vanilla ice cream) balances the flavor perfectly. "My STP is altogether deeper and darker than the original version," Lawson writes in At My Table. "It is still sweet, but the dark brown sugar and molasses give it an almost savage intensity. It seems redolent of ginger, cloves, allspice — and yet none of these spices are used. It's a miracle. I don't understand it — but then, miracles are not to be questioned. It shouldn't be eaten piping hot, but warm; once the sponge has been topped with a glaze of the sauce, and has had its 30 minutes' waiting time, it will be at optimum temperature."What is unsulfured molasses? Molasses falls into two primary categories: sulfured and unsulfured, with each available in light, dark, and blackstrap varieties depending on how much sugar has been extracted during processing. Sulfured molasses is made from immature sugar cane and treated with sulfur dioxide to preserve it before refining, which can impart slightly chemical or off flavors. Unsulfured molasses, by contrast, is produced from fully ripened sugar cane and requires no preservatives, resulting in a cleaner, more straightforward sweetness. For that reason, unsulfured molasses is generally preferred by bakers and cooks, and is the type most commonly found on grocery store shelves. Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen Chewy and sticky Medjool dates work best here, but any dried date will do."You will find it easier to measure out the molasses if you run your spoon under a hot tap first," writes Lawson.This recipe makes about two cups of sauce.Nigella Lawson's Sticky Toffee PuddingFrom Food & Wine MagazineActive Time: 30 mins.Total Time: 1 hour 30 mins.Servings: 9Ingredients:Cake12 large medjool dates (about 7 ounces or 1 packed cup), pitted and roughly chopped3/4 cup plus 1 tablespoon boiling water1 teaspoon baking soda5 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened, plus more for greasing2 tablespoons unsulfured light molasses1/4 cup packed dark brown sugar2 large eggs, at room temperature1 1/4 cups all-purpose flour

national.title: Recipe: Pecan Pie Bars
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Pecan pie bars have all the virtues of pecan pie without the fuss of rolling out a crust — and they're great for feeding a crowd.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Sarah Jordan.These tender and delicious pecan pie bars from pastry chef Sarah Jordan have an effortless press-in shortbread crust and a simple, custard-like filling packed with pecans. Unlike their pie counterpart, the bars' filling-to-crust ratio is fairly even, which helps to balance the sweetness of the corn syrup and dark brown sugar. Pecan pie bars are a great option when you have a lot of guests, whether it's for Thanksgiving or any other fall or winter festivities: Cut them into finger food–sized squares as part of a larger dessert spread or cookie table, or size them more generously for a main-event dessert. They also make a great take-home gift. Frequently Asked QuestionsIs there a difference between light corn syrup and dark corn syrup? The two main types of corn syrup differ in both appearance and flavor. Light corn syrup, called for in these pecan pie bars, is typically just corn syrup with some added salt and vanilla flavoring. It will look nearly clear. Dark corn syrup, on the other hand, has the addition of "refiner's syrup," also sometimes called "golden syrup" or "light treacle," a byproduct of sugar production that's somewhat similar to molasses, but more delicate in flavor. Dark corn syrup has a deeper, more caramel flavor, and is also darker in color. How do you prevent the bottom crust from getting soggy? Prebaking your pie dough fully ("blind baking") or partially ("parbaking") before adding the filling is a tried-and-true insurance against soggy pie bottoms, reinforcing the crust to withstand the liquids from custards, syrups, or juicy fruits. These easy pecan pie bars use Jordan's baked press-in crust, which provides a flaky and tender result with zero rolling involved. Make sure to press the dough into the pan in an even layer for a consistent bake, and feel free to use a layer of plastic wrap when pressing to keep your fingers clean. Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen The largest pecans, called "mammoth" (approximately 200 to 250 halves per pound), make for the most striking presentation. Look for them in specialty food shops. If you'd like to amplify the nutty flavor of the pecans, you can lightly toast them before stirring them into the filling (but be sure to let them cool first). national.title: Recipe: Super-Savory Turkey Gravy
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Oyster sauce adds tons of umami flavor in this elevated turkey gravy for Thanksgiving.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Ann Taylor Pittman. Gravy is a uniting element on the Thanksgiving table. It's perfect for drizzling over juicy white meat and rich dark meat alike, brings savory notes when pooled on top of a mound of mashed potatoes, and invites you to dip a tender yeast roll into it. Ann Taylor Pittman uses two smart techniques to produce a gravy that is beautifully smooth and flavorful: First, she stirs umami-forward oyster sauce into the turkey drippings to boost taste and introduce salty-sweet complexity. She also relies on beurre manié to thicken and enrich the pan sauce. Beurre manié is similar to a roux, and a no-fail, lump-free way to thicken gravy. Combine equal parts softened butter and flour, and slowly whisk the mixture into the gravy until it thickens into a rich, silky consistency. If you're one of those people who is anxious about making gravy, try thinking of it as a pan sauce — one that uses the drippings and browned bits from a turkey cooked over aromatics in a rimmed baking sheet instead of from a skillet-seared steak. Once the turkey is done, build the sauce from the drippings. Release the fond (those browned bits) by pouring sherry into the sheet pan and scraping with a wooden spoon, then use that liquid as the backbone of the gravy. To keep things simple, use store-bought chicken stock to add volume to the gravy. It's a trick you'll want to use for future weeknight meals with pork, steak, or chicken. You can use drippings from any roast turkey for this gravy, but drippings from our Sesame-Ginger Spatchcocked Turkey deliver even more umami-packed flavor for what is arguably the best Thanksgiving dinner ever. national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Layers of tender Yukon Gold potatoes, fennel, and onion bake under a silky three-cheese cream sauce in this deeply savory gratin.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was developed by Cameron Beall and written by Breana Killeen.There's nearly as much fennel and onion as potato in this gratin from Blackberry Farm's Cameron Beall, and that generous proportion is what sets it apart. As the thinly sliced vegetables slowly bake, the onion and fennel soften until sweet and almost jammy, settling between layers of tender Yukon Gold potatoes. Fennel's pronounced anise flavor also mellows considerably with cooking, leaving behind a gentle sweetness that complements the potatoes rather than overpowering them.Cheddar, Gruyère, and Parmesan make the sauce especially special alongside the heavy cream, which produces a smooth, stable sauce as the gratin spends more than an hour in the oven. Seasoning the vegetables as you build the layers is equally important, ensuring the potatoes, fennel, and onion are flavorful from top to bottom. After baking, give the gratin 10 to 15 minutes to rest so the sauce settles before serving.Reach for a mandoline Potatoes, fennel, and onion cook at different rates, so slicing them consistently thin is essential for getting everything tender at the same time. A mandoline makes quick work of the job and produces far more uniform slices than most cooks can achieve with a knife. Always use the mandoline's hand guard, particularly as you approach the end of each vegetable. Stick with heavy cream This isn't the place to substitute milk or a lower-fat dairy product. Heavy cream has enough fat to help the cheese sauce remain smooth and stable through the long baking time; lower-fat alternatives are more prone to separating. national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: Roasted carrots and parsnips get sweetness from sorghum syrup, with toasted walnuts and fresh thyme adding crunch and a fresh finish.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by The Beall Family.At Blackberry Farm, regional ingredients have long been central to the kitchen. These glazed parsnips and carrots put one of the South's distinctive sweeteners to work in an exceptionally simple side dish. Sorghum syrup has a long history in Southern and Appalachian cooking, where sweet sorghum was grown and its juice pressed and boiled into a dark, intensely flavored syrup. Today, the Southeast — and Appalachia in particular — remains closely associated with sorghum syrup production. Choose similarly sized rootsMedium carrots and parsnips are ideal because they can often be roasted whole, making for a striking presentation while helping the vegetables retain their texture. If some are noticeably thicker, halve or quarter them lengthwise to create pieces of comparable diameter. Avoid especially large parsnips when possible: Mature specimens can develop a tough, fibrous core. Smaller and medium-size parsnips tend to be more tender. Do you need to peel carrots and parsnips before roasting? Not strictly, but peeling is useful here for an even appearance and texture. Young roots with thin skins can simply be scrubbed well, while larger or older parsnips are better peeled (and possibly halved) because their exterior can become tougher. What is sorghum syrup? Sorghum syrup is a dark, pourable sweetener made by pressing the juice from sweet sorghum stalks and cooking it down until thick. Its flavor is rich, earthy, and slightly malty. Look for it at specialty grocers, Southern markets, or online. Substitute cane syrup, honey, or pure maple syrup instead. national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: White wine cuts through a rich Parmesan cream sauce in this holiday-worthy side of tender lacinato kale, sweet shallots, and plenty of garlic.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was developed by The Beall Family and written by Breana Killeen.Creamed spinach may be the steakhouse standard, but this creamed kale from the Beall family at Blackberry Farm makes a persuasive case for switching up the greens. Lacinato kale has considerably more structure than spinach, so even after sautéing and baking in a rich Parmesan cream sauce, the leaves retain a pleasant chew rather than disappearing into the sauce. Other versions of creamed kale similarly take advantage of kale's sturdy texture in rich cream sauces. It's an especially useful side for a holiday menu because the entire dish can be assembled a day in advance and baked just before dinner.Can you use frozen kale for creamed kale?Use freshly grated Parmesan rather than pre-grated cheese for the smoothest sauce. After the shallots and garlic soften, the white wine loosens the flavorful browned bits from the skillet and cooks down before the butter and cream are added. Stir most of the Parmesan directly into the cream until melted, then reserve the remainder for the top. Opt for freshly grated Parmesan cheese Use freshly grated Parmesan rather than pre-grated cheese for the smoothest sauce. After the shallots and garlic soften, the white wine loosens the flavorful browned bits from the skillet and cooks down before the butter and cream are added. Stir most of the Parmesan directly into the cream until melted, then reserve the remainder for the top. Notes From the Food & Wine Test Kitchen Add the kale by the handful rather than trying to fit it into the skillet all at once; each batch quickly wilts and makes room for the next.Grate the Parmesan yourself for the best melting consistency and a smooth, cohesive cream sauce.Let the creamed kale rest for about 10 minutes after baking so the sauce has time to settle and thicken slightly before serving.Creamed KaleFrom Food & Wine MagazineActive Time: 50 mins.Total Time: 1 hour 25 mins.Servings: 6-8Ingredients:5 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, divided2 pounds lacinato kale (3 to 4 bunches), stemmed and chopped (about 16 packed cups)1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, divided2 cups thinly sliced shallots (about 5 large shallots)12 garlic cloves, minced (about 1/4 cup)1/2 cup (4 ounces) dry white wine2 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more for baking dish1 cup heavy cream1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg1/4 teas

national.summary: James Beard Award-winner Sallie Ann Robinson, born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors.
national.body: In her 2019 cookbook "Sallie Ann Robinson's Kitchen: Food and Family Lore from the Lowcountry" (published by University Press of Florida), Sallie Ann Robinson, a chef and food writer born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors. She offers "Sunday Morning" viewers a collard greens recipe.She writes: "Many folks have never combined these two vegetables, but they go together well. Crunchy cabbage and silky collards are complementary flavors and textures."Collard Greens & Cabbage with Smoke Neck Bonesby Sallie Ann Robinson Serves 8-10Ingredients:3 pieces smoked pork neck bone (or smoked turkey wings)1 small bunch collard greens, picked over (remove any dead leaves), destemmed, and cut into 2 or 3 pieces1 large sweet onion, diced1 small cabbage, cut into 2-inch pieces1 tablespoon salt1 tablespoon pepperDirections:Fill a large pot half full of water, add the smoked neck bones, and bring to a boil over medium-high heat. Cook for 25 to 30 minutes, then drain off the water and return the meat to the pot, along with 3 cups hot water, and bring to a boil again. Cook for 20 to 30 minutes. While the meat is cooking, wash the collard leaves several times in warm water, and drain in a colander. When the meat is almost tender, add the collards and the onion. Season with salt and pepper, decrease the heat to medium, cover, and simmer, stirring on occasion, for 1 hour. Next add the cabbage and more water if needed, and cook for 30 to 45 minutes, until the cabbage is as tender as you like it. Keep warm over low heat until ready to serve. Serve with the cooking liquid, or potlikker. From "Sallie Ann Robinson's Kitchen: Food and Family Lore from the Lowcountry" by Sallie Ann Robinson. Copyright 2019 by Sallie Ann Robinson. national.title: Recipe: Triple-Pickle Cheese Ball
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: A trio of pickles and a crunchy potato chip coating give this cheese ball plenty of tang and texture.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was developed by Ann Taylor Pittman and written by Craig Ruff.This cheese ball turns a trio of briny favorites into a lively party appetizer that takes just 15 minutes to put together. Dill pickles provide their classic cucumber tang, peperoncini contribute a vinegary bite, and pickled jalapeños bring a measured kick. Folded into a base of cream cheese and extra-sharp cheddar, that layered triple-pickle brightness balances every bite. Fresh dill adds an herbal lift, while scallions, garlic powder, and onion powder lend ranch-inspired depth. The finishing touch is especially smart: Instead of the chopped nuts that traditionally coat many cheese balls, this one gets rolled in crushed potato chips. Their sturdy crunch is a playful contrast to the creamy interior and doubles down on all those salty flavors inside.There's no mandatory chilling period, so the cheese ball can go from mixing bowl to platter in minutes. Serve it with additional chips and crackers, or build out the platter with crisp crudités. Either way, expect this cheese ball to draw a crowd around the snack table. Frequently Asked QuestionsCan I substitute other pickles? Yes, you can substitute other pickles, such as bread-and-butter pickles, cornichons, peppadews, or banana peppers. Use an equal amount, drain them well, and chop them finely so the cheese ball doesn't become watery. Can I use a different type of chip? This recipe calls for kettle-cooked potato chips, but crackers, pretzel crisps, bagel chips, or toasted baguette slices would also work well. For a fresh option, serve it with crudités such as celery sticks, cucumber slices, bell pepper strips, radishes, or endive leaves. Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen A stand mixer works best for the thick cheese mixture. If you're making this recipe without one, beat the cream cheese and seasonings with a hand mixer, then fold in the cheddar and pickles with a stiff spatula.Place the chips in a large ziplock plastic bag, and crush them into coarse crumbs with your hands or a rolling pin. Avoid pulverizing them so they retain plenty of crunch.Wait to roll the cheese ball in the potato chips until just before serving. national.body: Award-winning actor Tony Shalhoub's new book, "We Thought They'd Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family" (written with Josie Adams, and published by Gallery Books), offers reflections on the role of food in his family reunions, along with recipes. He offers "Sunday Morning" viewers a story about a traditional bread – and tips on how to make it:Although this Middle Eastern staple is commonly called "manakeesh" or "za'atar bread," as kids, we always referred to it as "dirty bread." That moniker grew out of exactly how it looked to us, smeared with a dark, gritty, bespeckled oily coating. We loved homemade flatbread that was warm and soft, cool and crispy, drizzled with honey, spread with jam, dipped in labneh, or drenched in honey and jam and labneh. We also loved it wrapped around fresh greens or rolled into a cone and filled with hummus or Greek olives. What we could not understand was why the adults would take a perfectly perfect piece of flatbread and slather it with this slightly tart, slightly bitter, slightly grainy, super pungent "topsoil." To us, this was not so much gilding the lily as it was graveling the lily. My mother's soothing assurances that it was an "acquired taste" were always greeted with a collective eye roll. Yeah, right. ...And then, one day ... it just happened! One by one, as each of us reached a certain age or a certain stage—or a certain level of hunger—the penny dropped. Maybe it was the only snack within reach. Maybe it started with a dare. national.title: Recipe: Sallie Ann Robinson's Sweet Potato Cornbread
national.summary: The James Beard Award-winner, born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors.
national.body: In her 2019 cookbook "Sallie Ann Robinson's Kitchen: Food and Family Lore from the Lowcountry" (published by University Press of Florida), Sallie Ann Robinson, a chef and food writer born and raised on Daufuskie Island off the coast of South Carolina, shares recipes that celebrate the culinary heritage of her Gullah and Indigenous American ancestors. She offers "Sunday Morning" viewers her recipe for Sweet Potato Cornbread.Robinson writes: "Oh, how I remember those days when it was time to harvest the sweet potatoes and cook them. So many different dishes! And as simple as it may sound, this recipe was a favorite in our house."Sweet Potato Cornbreadby Sallie Ann Robinson Serves 8-10Ingredients:1 teaspoon salt4 to 5 sweet potatoes, skin on, cut into 3 pieces each4 cups yellow self-rising cornmeal1 cup self-rising flour3 large eggs, beaten2 cups whole milk1 cup evaporated milk1 1/2 cups sugar2 teaspoons vanilla extract1 cup molasses1 cup (2 sticks) butter, meltedDirections:Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Half fill a large pot with water and add the salt and sweet potatoes. Over medium-high heat, bring to a boil and cool for 30 minutes. The potatoes will still be firm. Drain and set aside to cool, then peel them. In a large bowl, combine the cornmeal and flour. In a medium bowl, combine the eggs, whole milk, evaporate milk, sugar, vanilla, molasses, and ¾ cup of the butter. Using a hand mixer on medium speed, or a spoon, mix well until the sugar is dissolved. Fold in the sweet potatoes. Fold the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients and combine well. Try not to break up the sweet potatoes. Add the remaining ¼ cup butter to a 9-by-13-inch baking pan or a large skillet, and place in the oven until hot. Pour the batter into the heated pan, leaving ½ inch space at the top for room to rise. Bake for 45 minutes to 1 hour, until the top is slightly browned and a toothpick inserted in the center of the cornbread comes out clean. Let cool, then slice and serve. From "Sallie Ann Robinson's Kitchen: Food and Family Lore from the Lowcountry" by Sallie Ann Robinson. Copyright 2019 by Sallie Ann Robinson. Published by University Press of Florida. national.title: Recipe: Gougères with Smoked Salmon, Caviar and Prosciutto
national.summary: From the editors of Food & Wine: These cheesy puffs look fancy, but come together in minutes to make any snack feel like an occasion.
national.body: This recipe, courtesy of Food & Wine Magazine, was by Chandra Ram.Gougères are one of those snacks that deliver a lot of flavor but are easy to make. A pâte à choux, or cream puff dough, forms the base of the gougères. When making the dough, be sure to cook it on the stove until it pulls away from the sides of the pot; cooking out the water helps the gougères rise and get crispy when they bake. Then, mix the dough for a couple of minutes to let it cool slightly before adding the eggs. Once the dough is ready, you can pipe it onto a baking sheet and bake immediately, or freeze the mounds of dough and keep them in your back pocket for a last-minute cocktail party or snack situation (frozen gougères can bake straight from the freezer; they will need an extra minute or two in the oven). You can make these as small or large as you like; large gougères can stand in for dinner rolls or even serve as the base for an eggs Benedict at brunch. And have fun experimenting with them. These gougères are made with grated Gruyère cheese and thyme leaves, but you can swap in another grated hard cheese, or use spices and other herbs. We topped these with slivers of prosciutto and smoked salmon and dollops of caviar and crème fraîche, but any toppings will do. Or, simply eat them plain — they shine on their own. national.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
national.summary: The Russian embassy in Denmark has denied the allegation, which has led to Russia's defence attaché being expelled.
national.body:
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.

Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.

Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.

Russia's embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.

In a statement, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".

Russian state media cite the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".

In a statement on Saturday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "I strongly condemn the assassination attempt against a US-Ukrainian citizen in Denmark, orchestrated by Russian intelligence services.

"This was an attack on EU soil. And it is unacceptable," she said, adding that "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real."

national.title: 5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
national.summary: Don't let your work troubles follow you home. Psychologist Guy Winch shares techniques to help you stop ruminating about your nine-to-five, so you can focus on what really matters.
national.body:
Psychologist Guy Winch, author of Mind Over Grind , shares techniques to help you stop thinking about work when the day is over. Beck Harlan for NPR hide caption

If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You're still on the clock, says psychologist Guy Winch .

" Your workday only ends when you stop thinking about work," he says.

Life Kit Listen to the podcast version of this story here Winch, author of Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life , says it doesn't have to be this way. In his book, published this year, he shares strategies on how to reclaim your time, energy and attention if work takes up too much of your mental bandwidth.

"Very few of us sit through the evening reliving the glory of the joke that landed in the meeting," he says. "What we do spend hours on are when we get interrupted, dismissed, about the project we're behind on."

That kind of ruminative thinking can have negative effects on our health . Research has shown that it activates our stress response, contributes to poor sleep and eating and, over time, can increase our risks for cardiovascular disease and depression.

Winch, co-host of the podcast Dear Therapists , shares quick strategies you can try if work is taking over your life.

Let's say you're trying to focus on your kid's volleyball game but all you can think about is how your colleague keeps taking credit for your work.

national.title: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
national.summary: AI stocks — and the broader markets — got pummeled this week, raising major concerns about the financial system and the wider economy. Here's what to know.
national.body:
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.

Understanding AI Anthropic and OpenAI CEOs call for AI development to slow down, OpenAI to delay IPO AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.

Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing

Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.

Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.

It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.

Technology U.S. tightens controls on remote access to AI technology amid Nvidia fallout Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.

national.title: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
national.summary: A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
national.body:
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.

It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.

Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.

Voting Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College . So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.

There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.

"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.

Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.

So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.

national.title: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
national.summary: Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
national.body:
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.

Technology Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO "There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."

Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.

The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.

But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.

The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.

Understanding AI California sues OpenAI over hacking risks Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."

Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.

national.title: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
national.summary: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
national.body:
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run through the night, as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.

In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

Separately, the Africa Group are fighting to get commitments on more money for adaptation, saying they did not come to the COP "to beg".

A new and potentially final agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.

More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged

Published 1 day ago Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.

"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.

national.title: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
national.summary: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
national.body:
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

national.title: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
national.summary: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
national.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.

This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.

It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.

In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .

national.title: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
national.summary: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.
national.body:
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.

The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.

Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.

"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."

Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."

Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.

national.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
national.summary: Earlier this week, Trump greeted Putin ahead of a meeting in China and said the pair have a "great relationship".
national.body:
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.

Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

national.title: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
national.summary: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground. U.N.-backed talks in Geneva ended Saturday with an agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
national.body:
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.

Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.

The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a "significant achievement" but acknowledged a "glass half full or half empty" scenario, citing Guterres' hopes for a legally binding deal this year.

Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.

Stop Killer Robots lamented a "watered-down mandate," and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to "pushing the can down the road for two more years."

They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: "States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities."

Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.

national.title: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
national.summary: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
national.body:
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.

The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial .

Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.

Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

national.title: Judge approves $7.25bn settlement for Roundup weedkiller cancer claims
national.summary: The settlement will be paid by Bayer to users who already have non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.
national.body:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn (£5.5bn) settlement stemming from lawsuits ⁠alleging that Bayer's weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.

Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate".

Bayer, the German bio-tech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.

The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.

The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.

The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.

Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.

Some attorneys had objected to the settlement funds, arguing they were not enough, but the judge said he did not want to delay payouts to sick victims.

national.title: Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
national.summary: At the funeral for the 15-year-old who was fatally shot last month, Mamdani spoke alongside the boy's father and civil rights leaders.
national.body:
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.

Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.

"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."

"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.

His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.

Earlier this month, she told the BBC that she wanted "justice for my son", a sentiment echoed at Friday's service.

Officials have said they are exploring several motives. Frimpong's family has said he experienced bullying at school, which police said they were investigating.

Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

national.title: They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop
national.summary: How convicted fraudsters made millions from detained immigrants, evaded efforts to shut down their bail business and left migrants behind bars.
national.body:
Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

Top aviation officials within the Trump administration have previously said the cause was related to old equipment overloading, as well as updates to systems.
